meta.title: From Ground to In-Orbit: Enabling Real-Time On-Board Anomaly Detection with ATHMoS
meta.authorsHtml: Kathrin Helmsauer<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Clemens Schefels<sup>1</sup>, Leonard Schlag<sup>1</sup>, Christian Stirm<sup>1</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: The Automated Telemetry Health Monitoring System (ATHMoS) has been operational at the German Space Operations Center (GSOC) since 2022 as a semi-supervised novelty detection framework for spacecraft telemetry, enabling the detection of previously unseen system states without labeled anomaly data. This paper presents the systematic transformation of ATHMoS from a batch-oriented ground analysis tool to a real-time onboard implementation (ATHMoS-RT). We introduce architectural and algorithmic adaptations that enable deployment at the edge under strict safety and computational constraints, while preserving statistical traceability and human oversight. A comparative analysis of ground and onboard configurations reveals how simplified workflows can maintain reliable detection despite limited compute resources. This transition significantly reduces the time-to-detection by removing dependencies on ground-station contact, allowing operators to prepare for anomalies in real-time before the next scheduled satellite pass.

blocks.html: Modern satellites generate vast volumes of housekeeping telemetry, often comprising tens of thousands of parameters that must be continuously monitored to ensure mission safety and performance. Traditional monitoring approaches, such as limit checks or rule-based systems, reliably detect threshold violations but may fail to identify subtle deviations or previously unseen behaviors. As mission complexity and autonomy requirements increase, data-driven anomaly detection is becoming an essential component of space operations.

At the German Space Operations Center (GSOC) of the German Aerospace Center (DLR), this challenge is addressed through the Automated Telemetry Health Monitoring System (ATHMoS). This semi-supervised novelty detection framework utilizes intrinsic dimensionality–driven outlier probabilities (OPVID) to model nominal spacecraft behavior directly from historical telemetry. By avoiding reliance on labeled anomaly data, it enables the detection of previously unseen system states. Since 2022, ATHMoS has been deployed operationally on multiple missions, supporting engineers in identifying statistically novel behavior within the ground segment.

ATHMoS was first developed as a ground-based tool, benefiting from the vast data and computing resources available at GSOC. Given its operational maturity, extending the system to the onboard segment is a strategic move toward achieving greater autonomy and faster anomaly awareness. As mission concepts shift toward edge computing, often faced with intermittent ground contact and limited bandwidth, deploying these monitoring capabilities directly on board becomes essential. However, this requires a careful redesign of the architecture to balance real-time execution with the need for robustness.

Despite its operational success on the ground, two primary limitations persist. First, there is a significant temporal gap between anomaly occurrence and detection due to irregular satellite contact and the nature of data dump schedules. Second, while ATHMoS identifies novelties, many ground-detected anomalies are already captured by traditional static limit checks. This suggests that the true added value of novelty detection is maximized when shifted to the onboard segment, where real-time awareness allows for immediate reactions and enables engineers to prepare for potential issues before the next scheduled groundstation pass.

This paper presents the evolution of ATHMoS from a ground-based operational monitoring service to a real-time, onboard-capable anomaly detection system. We describe its current operational integration at GSOC, the algorithmic and architectural adaptations enabling its onboard variant (ATHMoS-RT), and validation results including planned in-orbit demonstrations within the Stellar Apps framework. By comparing ground and onboard configurations, we highlight the trade-offs between real-time execution and bounded resource usage, demonstrating how novelty detection can serve as a controlled and explainable entry point for AI-based edge computing in safety-critical spacecraft systems.

Several space agencies and research groups have explored machine learning–based telemetry monitoring on ground and on board. The Centre national d’études spatiales (CNES) developed NOSTRADAMUS, an operational One-Class SVM–based anomaly detection system deployed on multiple missions for over six years, and extended it through the SESAM experiment to demonstrate onboard execution and potential interaction with FDIR for autonomous reconfiguration [1]. Supervised learning approaches have also been applied to OPS-SAT telemetry [2], targeting predefined anomaly classes using labeled datasets. More recently, hardware-accelerated streaming architectures have been proposed for continuous onboard anomaly detection with concept drift handling and adaptive model updates [3].

While these approaches demonstrate the feasibility of AI-based telemetry monitoring, they often rely on supervised classification or model-centric representations of nominal behavior. In contrast, ATHMoS follows a semi-supervised novelty detection paradigm that models nominal spacecraft behavior using intrinsic dimensionality–based statistics, enabling controlled model updates, statistical traceability, and stable integration into operational engineering workflows.

blocks.title: Novelty Detection in Ground Operations at GSOC: ATHMoS

blocks.html: ATHMoS has been operating as a ground-based anomaly detection system at GSOC since 2022 and has matured from a research prototype [4] into a stable operational tool [5]. Over the past years, it has been integrated into routine mission operations and continuously refined based on practical experience and direct feedback from spacecraft operators and subsystem engineers [6]. This section provides a concise overview of the current operational setup and overall workflow. For the mathematical details of the algorithm, we refer the reader to [4].

ATHMoS is a semi-supervised anomaly detection framework designed to identify novel behavior in satellite housekeeping telemetry. Rather than relying on predefined thresholds or fault signatures, the system models nominal behavior directly from historical data and flags deviations based on statistical novelty. This design makes it particularly suitable for missions with large parameter sets, limited or no labeled data, and evolving operational conditions.
ATHMoS operates on a per-parameter basis and follows a modular workflow consisting of data pre-processing, feature extraction, model training (c.f. Figure 1), and model inference (c.f. Figure 2).

As a first step, parameters are automatically classified into different types as visualized in Figure 3, i.e. into continuous parameters, general discrete parameters, counters, and wiggly counters, enabling parameter-specific feature extraction tailored to the statistical characteristics of each signal. In our preprocessing steps, raw telemetry is cleaned and standardized, including gap handling and interpolation to ensure uniform time sampling.

Feature extraction is performed using a sliding-window approach. For low Earth orbit missions, ATHMoS typically computes feature vectors over 90-minute windows, which roughly encompasses one orbit of LEO satellites, with a 30minute step size, capturing both short-term dynamics and orbital periodicity. Depending on the parameter type, features are derived from raw values, smoothed signals, noise components, or step-based representations. These feature vectors form the basis for both training and inference.

The initial model training is performed primarily in an unsupervised manner using unlabeled telemetry data. While the system can incorporate ground-truth labels should they be available, it does not require them. This is a critical advantage given that labeled anomaly datasets are typically unavailable for most missions. To prevent anomalies present in the historical data from contaminating the model, ATHMoS applies a clustering based on Density- Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DB- SCAN, [7]), as can be seen in Figure 4, to filter out outlier feature vectors, retaining only sufficiently large clusters that represent recurring nominal behavior. On this filtered dataset, ATHMoS builds a k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) representation and computes intrinsic dimensionality–based statistics, which is described by the pseudo-code in Figure 5. Novelty during inference is quantified using the Outlier Probability via Intrinsic Dimension (OPVID, c.f. [4, Sec. II]) as illustrated in Figure 6, which measures how strongly a new feature vector deviates from the learned nominal structure.

Operationally, ATHMoS employs a dual-model strategy consisting of a long-term model (one year) capturing seasonal and historical behavior and a short-term model (thirty days) focusing on short-term dynamics. Each model produces an independent novelty scores allowing the system to detect sudden deviations, recent behavioral shifts, and long-term drifts. This dual-perspective approach allows ATHMoS to detect relevant anomalies automatically while supporting engineers in prioritizing critical events. To ensure high precision, detected novelties are post-processed using consistency checks to suppress isolated detections and reduce false positives before being presented to our engineers through the Visualization and Data Analysis (ViDA [8, 9]) framework as seen in the screenshot in Figure 7.

Furthermore, we have added a reclassification workflow to use our engineers’ feedback in our semi-supervised approach. Engineers are now able to mark detected novelties as nominal in the ViDA frontend, which can then be incorporated in subsequent model retraining. This ensures that recurring non-critical events, such as maneuvers or maintenance operations, do not trigger unnecessary alerts.

Since its initial deployment, ATHMoS has been continuously enhanced based on operational experience. In its current form, the system serves as a robust and extensible baseline for anomaly detection in ground operations and provides the foundation for the real-time and on-board extensions as discussed in the subsequent sections.

blocks.title: Results: Adapting ATHMoS for Real-Time and On-Board Use

blocks.html: Transitioning ATHMoS from ground-based operations to an onboard environment requires a streamlined workflow adapted to constrained computing power and latency constraints of satellites. In this mode, several of the processing steps are simplified compared to the on-ground version of ATHMoS, while still ensuring a reliable and fast detection of novelties.

For the actual deployment of our code on board the satellites, we are relying on the Stellar Apps software platform, which is described in Section 4.1. We explain the simplified ATHMoS workflow, which we are planning to use on-board, in Section 4.2

blocks.title: Stellar Apps: Concept for On-Board AI

blocks.html: The transition from ground-based analysis to real-time on-board anomaly detection requires a different deployment paradigm for artificial intelligence in space systems. Traditional spacecraft software architectures are tightly coupled to hardware and mission-critical functions, limiting their suitability for adaptive, data-driven algorithms. At the same time, increasing autonomy requirements, higher data volumes, and limited downlink availability motivate processing telemetry directly on board.

Recent approaches therefore favor modular, applicationcentric execution environments that decouple AI services from core flight software. The Stellar Apps software platform [10] implements this concept by providing a standardized execution environment with strong application isolation, controlled resource access via defined APIs, real-time support, and cybersecurity safeguards. This architecture enables edge computing on board while preserving mission safety.

Within this platform, anomaly detection is a suitable first AI application, as it provides advisory early-warning information without issuing control commands. ATHMoS aligns well with this approach: its modular workflow and separation of training and inference facilitate adaptation to a resource-constrained, real-time onboard execution. The following section outlines the required modifications for the real-time adaption of ATHMoS, ATHMoS-RT.

blocks.caption: The three main components of Stellar Apps, as described in [10]: 1) the application developer; 2) the trusted ground interface; and 3) the space segment.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: To operate within limited onboard resources, the streamlined ATHMoS workflow retains only the components required for real-time inference. To ensure high responsiveness and lightweight signal conditioning, the onboard processing utilizes short sliding windows. Bounded memory usage is primarily achieved by reducing the model’s spatial footprint; specifically, the training horizon is limited to several weeks rather than a full year, and a compact feature set with reduced dimensionality is employed. This optimized feature vector is tailored for continuous parameters to ensure efficient computation.

The real-time variant maintains a single model covering just a few weeks of telemetry using the minimal training workflow in Figure 9. Incoming data is evaluated in real-time using short sliding windows of a few minutes, c.f. Figure 10. Consistent with the training workflow, the inference workflow requires no additional preprocessing beyond the feature computation itself. To finalize a detection, the system applies a persistence check, verifying that the ATHMoS novelty scores remain elevated across several subsequent overlapping windows. This enables timely detection of anomalies while keeping computational overhead minimal.

To maintain operational efficiency, the system continuously monitors model performance for degradation stemming from seasonal effects not contained in the training data, evolving spacecraft behavior or hardware aging. While the ground-based version of ATHMoS utilizes a full year of training data, the onboard variant is limited to a window of several weeks due to resource constraints. Consequently, ATHMoS-RT forgoes fixed retraining schedules in favor of a conditional approach; as illustrated in Figure 11, maintaining a stationary model leads to a measurable decline in detection quality over time.

blocks.caption: Drifting Temeletry Causing ATHMoS Detections. Blue is Telemetry, Red ATHMoS Novelty Score, Shaded Regions are ATHMoS Detections.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: While one could theoretically train higher-fidelity models on the ground and uplink them periodically, this approach is often impractical due to potentially long intervals between spacecraft contacts and the severely limited bandwidth of uplink channels. To ensure the model remains current without depending on frequent ground intervention, the workflow for ATHMoS-RT must therefore handle retraining autonomously.

This autonomy is realized through a dual-trigger strategy designed to maintain model accuracy without overloading subsystem engineers. First, retraining is triggered if there is a detectable increase in average novelty scores in the absence of explicit detections. Second, for cases where anomalies are explicitly detected, the system employs a controlled notification loop to prevent alert spamming: detections for any single parameter are muted for 24 hours following an initial trigger. If the anomaly persists beyond this window, a second notification is issued; if the state remains anomalous after this second alert, the system triggers a model retraining. This ensures that engineers are notified of persistent anomalies, confirmed by two distinct alerts separated by a 24-hour interval, without receiving redundant messages. This approach balances the requirement for human oversight with operational efficiency, allowing engineers to assess critical events before updates are applied.

Detected novelties are communicated immediately to ground operators via the Stellar Apps application On Board Data Analysis and Realtime Information System (ODARIS [11]), which issues alerts such as text messages. This shifts the operational paradigm from reactive analysis to proactive preparation, allowing engineers to investigate telemetry precursors and formulate mitigation strategies prior to the next satellite contact, thereby reducing the time-to-resolution for critical anomalies.

This real-time version of ATHMoS has been extensively tested and validated on historic data of DLR’s cubesat Euglena and Combined Regenerative Organic-Food Production in Space (Eu:CROPIS). In addition, we are planning a technology demonstration of ATHMoS-RT in the Stellar Apps software platform on the Cubesat to Accommodate Payloads and Technology Experiments (CAPTn-1), which is scheduled to launch in early 2027. More missions are planned for the future.

Migrating ATHMoS from ground-based monitoring to real-time onboard execution changes the operational context under which the system operates. While the intrinsic dimensionality–based novelty detection principle remains unchanged, the surrounding workflow design must account for limited computational resources, safety requirements, and real-time behavior.

As ATHMoS has now reached a level of operational maturity at GSOC, the system is transitioning into a maintenance phase for ground operations. This stability provides the necessary foundation to pivot development efforts toward the more challenging environment of real-time on-board execution.

On the ground, ATHMoS benefits from extensive preprocessing, long historical training datasets, and comparatively unconstrained computing resources. The one-year training horizon, clustering-based filtering, and rich feature set provide statistical robustness and fine-grained discrimination between nominal and anomalous behavior.

Conversely, the onboard design prioritizes bounded complexity and predictable execution. The training horizon is reduced to a few weeks, preprocessing is simplified, and clustering-based filtering is omitted. A compact feature set ensures fast inference with limited memory and processing demand. These adjustments reduce statistical depth but enable timely early-warning detection under strict re-source constraints. Crucially, this trade-off is justified by the elimination of the temporal gap inherent in ground operations; by shifting the computation to the edge, the system removes the dependency on irregular data dumps, providing immediate awareness of anomalies as they occur.

Adapting models onboard introduces challenges related to drift and stability. Configuration changes, aging effects, or mission phase transitions may degrade performance if the model is not updated. Conversely, frequent retraining risks incorporating anomalous behavior before ground engineers can assess it.

ATHMoS-RT therefore preserves a controlled retraining strategy, monitoring model performance while ensuring sufficient time for human evaluation. The system enhances situational awareness without autonomously redefining nominal behavior.

On-board AI must remain strictly separated from missioncritical flight software. By operating as an isolated application within an application-centric software platform such as Stellar Apps, ATHMoS-RT maintains controlled interfaces and can be monitored or deactivated independently. As an advisory early-warning system rather than a control mechanism, anomaly detection provides a low-risk entry point for validating edge AI in safety-critical spacecraft environments.

The current onboard implementation is intentionally conservative, focusing on continuous parameters and a single adaptive model to ensure real-time capability. Long-term in-orbit evaluation across mission phases remains ongoing.

While ground-based novelty detection often overlaps with existing static limit checks, the move to an onboard architecture shifts the utility of ATHMoS from retrospective verification to proactive preparation. Future work will investigate broader parameter coverage, enhanced onboard data utilization, and more advanced response mechanisms such as higher on-board data utilization, prioritized data downlink, adaptive monitoring strategies, and integration with additional on-board decision-support modules. In the longer term, such developments may support more proactive spacecraft health management while maintaining operational control and safety.

We also acknowledge the Stellar Apps development team for their collaboration and technical support in enabling the on-board implementation of ATHMoS-RT.
